hints: Think about what varies between the hydrocarbon molecules in crude oil, such as chain length and molecular size.
Recall which intermolecular force acts between non-polar alkane molecules and what has to be overcome when they boil.
walkthrough:
Picture what is different about the molecules**
Crude oil is not one compound. It contains alkanes from very short chains like $\text{C}_5$ up to very long chains like $\text{C}_{40}$. That means the molecules have very different relative molecular masses and very different total numbers of electrons.

Name the only forces that matter here**
Alkanes are non-polar, so there is no hydrogen bonding and no permanent dipole-dipole attraction. When liquid alkane boils you do not break $\text{C-C}$ or $\text{C-H}$ covalent bonds, you only separate whole molecules from each other. That means you are only overcoming London dispersion forces between molecules.

Link electrons to strength to boiling point**
A larger molecule with more electrons is more easily polarised, so it forms stronger temporary dipoles and stronger London forces. More thermal energy is needed to pull those molecules apart, so boiling point is higher. Because each hydrocarbon has a different electron count, each has a different London force strength and a different boiling point, which is why fractional distillation can separate them.

Final answer: Different hydrocarbon molecules have different chain lengths and different numbers of electrons.
Therefore they have different strengths of London dispersion (induced dipole-dipole) forces between molecules, so different amounts of energy are needed to separate them, giving different boiling points.

hints: Compare the supply of long chain fractions from distillation with the market demand for petrol and for alkenes.
walkthrough:
Think supply versus demand**
Fractional distillation gives a lot of long chain fractions like fuel oil and bitumen for which demand is low, but not enough petrol fraction and alkenes for which demand is very high. Cracking breaks a low demand, low value long chain alkane into shorter, more useful molecules. You get short chain alkanes for petrol and alkenes like ethene and propene as feedstock for polymers and other chemicals.
Final answer: To produce more useful, higher demand, more valuable shorter chain alkanes and alkenes from excess low demand long chain hydrocarbons.

hints: Start with $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{26}$ on the left and $2\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ plus one unknown hydrocarbon on the right, then balance C and H to find the unknown.
walkthrough:
Balance by subtraction**
Write the skeleton: $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{26} \rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{unknown}$. For carbon: $12 - (2 \times 2) = 8$ carbons left. For hydrogen: $26 - (2 \times 4) = 18$ hydrogens left. So the other product is $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}$. The full balanced equation is $$\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{26} \rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}$$

hints: Recall the name of the polymerisation in which many alkene monomers join by opening the C=C double bond with no other product.
walkthrough:
Spot the monomer type**
Ethene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$, is an alkene. When alkenes join together by breaking the pi bond of the $\text{C=C}$ and forming new $\text{C-C}$ single bonds between monomers, with the alkene as the only reactant and the polymer as the only product, the process is called addition polymerisation.

hints: Think about what happens if a plastic bag is left in the environment for decades and why landfill space is a problem.
Think about where the ethene monomer comes from and what happens if waste plastic is burned instead of recycled.
walkthrough:
Remember why plastic waste stays around**
Poly(ethene) has a long saturated carbon chain that microorganisms cannot break down, so it is non-biodegradable. If thrown away it fills landfill for hundreds of years, creates litter and visual pollution, and can entangle or be eaten by wildlife.

Link recycling to resources and pollution**
Making new poly(ethene) uses crude oil, which is non-renewable. Reusing and recycling conserves that resource and saves landfill space. It also avoids burning the plastic, which can release toxic gases such as carbon monoxide and polluting smoke.

Final answer: Poly(ethene) is non-biodegradable so persists in landfill and as litter, causing eyesore and harm to wildlife.
Reuse or recycling saves limited landfill space and conserves finite crude oil resources, and avoids harmful products from incineration.

hints: Isolate one repeat unit from the chain, it contains a $\text{CH}_2$ group plus a $\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{COOCH}_3)$ group joined by single bonds in the polymer backbone.
Recall how to convert that saturated two-carbon backbone section back to a monomer by re-forming a C=C double bond between the two backbone carbons.
walkthrough:
Find the repeating pair**
Look at the backbone: $-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{COOCH}_3)-$. That two-carbon unit repeats all along the chain. In addition polymerisation this comes from one alkene monomer, so those two backbone carbons were joined by a $\text{C=C}$ double bond in the monomer.

Draw the monomer fully displayed**
Put back the double bond: $\text{CH}_2=\text{C}$. Keep the same two side groups on the second carbon: a $\text{CH}_3$ group and a $\text{COOCH}_3$ ester group. So you draw $$\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{O}-\text{CH}_3$$ with every single and double bond shown and every H, C and O atom shown explicitly. Check that the $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-O-CH}_3$ part is fully displayed, that is what earns the second mark.

Final answer: Monomer is $\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{COOCH}_3$ shown fully displayed with all atoms and all bonds drawn, including $\text{C}=\text{O}$, $\text{C-O}$ and $\text{O-CH}_3$.
